query: Consider the following context: The recent perspective of multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), has emerged as a very promising area for material design. Additive manufacturing (AM) strategies have also been noted to provide additional strength to HEA systems. In the selected dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA system, an additional strength of approximately 300–400 MPa was achieved by adopting an additive manufacturing route as compared to its cast and wrought counterparts. However, the challenge of oxidation degradation always imposes a severe limitation for high-temperature applications in gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components. Hence, ensuring material sustainability, longevity, and integrity for high-temperature applications inevitably requires the exploration of the oxidation behavior of alloys. In that context, which method can be used for elucidating the mechanistic aspects and elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates on oxidation behavior, and why?

Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material. decision.trend: The trend in the research is focused on understanding the properties and behavior of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), particularly in terms of their oxidation resistance, mechanical strength, and microstructure. The studies have explored various processing techniques, such as additive manufacturing, spark plasma sintering, and laser powder bed fusion, to produce HEAs with improved properties. The research has also investigated the effects of alloy composition, grain size, and precipitation on the oxidation behavior and mechanical properties of HEAs.
decision.unsolved: One of the major challenges in the field of HEAs is understanding the oxidation behavior and degradation mechanisms of these alloys at high temperatures. The research has shown that HEAs can exhibit improved oxidation resistance compared to traditional alloys, but the underlying mechanisms are not yet fully understood. Additionally, the development of HEAs with balanced mechanical properties, such as strength, ductility, and toughness, remains a significant challenge.
decision.lever: transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT)
decision.why: The next step in understanding the oxidation behavior and degradation mechanisms of HEAs would be to employ advanced characterization techniques, such as TEM and APT, to investigate the microstructure and composition of HEAs at the nanoscale. These techniques would allow researchers to examine the distribution of elements, grain boundaries, and precipitates, and their role in determining the oxidation resistance and mechanical properties of HEAs.
